newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France denies eyeing Eramet assets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France denies eyeing Eramet assets.

text.p: The French government said on Tuesday it had no plans to strip part of the mining assets of nickel producer Eramet in New Caledonia as part of negotiations over mining reserves in the Pacific territory.
"It formally denies serious allegations that it might try to rob Eramet of part of its mining resources," the industry ministry said in a statement.
The statement calmed investors' concerns and helped lift the share price from a year low early on Tuesday of 247 francs. The shares were up 13.9 francs at 279.9 in mid-afternoon trade.
They had slumped on concerns that the French government might force Eramet -- which it controls with a 55 percent holding -- to sell part of its mining interest in New Caledonia.

Under a 1988 plan to quell separatist tensions in the French territory, France agreed to help redress the balance between the interests of the local Kanak people against those of French settlers ahead of a vote on independence set for 1998.

As part of the plan, France is widely expected to support a project by the pro-independence Kanak Socialist Liberation Front Party (FLNKS) and Canadian metals group Falconbridge to build a nickel plant in northern New Caledonia.
The plan would deal a blow to Eramet's expansion strategy in New Caledonia, as Eramet might be ordered to sell part or all of its Thiebaghi reserves to supply the new plant, analysts said.
Despite the government's pledge on Tuesday, investors including powerful British and U.S. financial institutions remained concerned about the group's future in New Caledonia.
Analysts said investors were worried that Eramet's highly regarded chairman, Yves Rambaud, might be replaced as he opposes any plan to reduce Eramet's mining assets in the region.
Eramet board members met on Tuesday to study a plan put forward by the state-controlled holding company Erap to turn Eramet into a company with supervisory and management boards.
The change, if cleared by the board, might have heralded the ouster of Rambaud. But in a statement issued after the meeting, Eramet said the board had decided to study the proposal.
Asked if this meant that Eramet's management team would stay on, a company spokesman said: "Yes indeed".
"Investors are furious that a government may use its 55 percent stake in a listed company to push through its political interests in New Caledonia," one analyst said,
"Whatever happens, the damage is done. The share is dead on the stock market," another analyst said.
The affair may also spell trouble for future privatisations if investors worry the government might ignore shareholders in the pursuit of its political interests, analysts said.
Eramet ranks third among world nickel producers. It plans to produce more than 60,000 tonnes of nickel by the year 2,000 from expected 1996 output of 53,000 tonnes.
The higher output was expected to come mostly from nickel facilities in New Caledonia, where Eramet recently decided to build a fifth rotary kiln at its Doniambo smelter,
It started to develop the Thiebaghi nickel deposit in early 1995 and hopes to reach a capacity of 24,000 tonnes.

One analyst suggested the government may offer to buy out minority shareholders, particularly if the stock remained low. But other analysts thought the prospect of "re-nationalisation" was highly unlikely.
